extracted.intended_audience: PTAB panels and administrative judges; PTAB Chief/Deputy Chief Judge; parties to remanded proceedings (petitioners, patent owners), and patent practitioners involved in remands from the Federal Circuit
extracted.subtask_description: Standard Operating Procedure for handling cases remanded from the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, providing timelines, meeting practices, and rules for allowing additional briefing, evidence, or hearings on remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six‑month goal for issuing decisions on remand
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has established a goal to issue decisions on remanded cases within six months of the Board’s receipt of the Federal Circuit’s mandate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mandate makes the judgment of the Federal Circuit final and releases jurisdiction of the remanded case to the Board. Certain scenarios may necessitate an extension of the six‑month goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early remand meeting with Chief/Deputy Chief Judge and panel
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chief Judge and/or the Deputy Chief Judge will discuss each remanded case with the panel before the issuance of the mandate, and panels are requested to schedule a meeting within thirty days of receiving notice of the Federal Circuit’s decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meetings may occur with delegates in lieu of the Chief/Deputy Chief Judge; the Chief Judge may expand the panel in accordance with SOP 1 (expected to be rare). The meeting is intended to identify and discuss potential issues early and is not intended to decide the likely substantive outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel preparation for remand meetings (Appendix 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels should be prepared to discuss issues presented by the Federal Circuit decision and expected procedures for preparing a remand decision; panels may (but are not required to) provide a short (e.g., not to exceed two pages), informal summary addressing relevant issues in advance of the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given early timing, the meeting should not address likely substantive outcomes. Panels should consider the general topics listed in Appendix 1 'if relevant to their particular remand.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential topics for remand meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Topics include: procedural history (including pre-appeal history and related appeals), outcome and rationale of the Federal Circuit decision, the issues on remand (procedural instructions and substantive issues), contemplated procedures for proceedings on remand (additional briefing, hearings, reopening the record), recommendation on panel expansion, and policy considerations including precedential designation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The panel should consider whether a decision on remand raises novel, evolving, or contentious issues of law or policy that might be suitable for precedential designation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party contact and meet-and-confer timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties in remanded trial cases are to contact the Board within ten (10) business days after the mandate issues to arrange a teleconference with the panel. Before the teleconference, the parties shall meet and confer in a reasonable and good faith attempt to propose a procedure on remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleconferences with the panel should take place within the first month after the mandate. Parties are encouraged to seek agreement on remand procedures including whether additional briefing is necessary, subject matter limitations, length and sequence of briefing, whether additional evidence or hearings should be permitted, schedules, and other procedural issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel retains ultimate authority to decide remand procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the panel shall consider procedures proposed by the parties, the panel ultimately will decide the procedures to be followed on remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The panel will determine whether to permit additional briefing, additional evidence (testimonial and documentary), and/or additional hearings following a remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations in choosing remand procedures (statutory and policy factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The panel will consider the scope of the remand as determined by the Federal Circuit and the 'effect . . . on the economy, the integrity of the patent system, the efficient administration of the Office, and the ability of the Office to timely complete proceedings.' (See 35 U.S.C. §§ 316(b), 326(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel should also weigh time and expense of permitting additional briefing/new evidence against the Board’s goal of timely decisions and the regulation goal to 'secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive resolution of every proceeding' (37 C.F.R. § 42.1(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing additional briefing on remand
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding whether to allow additional briefing, the panel will take into account whether the parties already have had an adequate opportunity to address the issues raised by the remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new or revised claim construction not previously considered or a change in the law usually justifies additional briefing. Additional briefing, when permitted, will normally be limited to the specific issues raised by the remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing additional evidence on remand
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, it will not be necessary to re‑open the evidentiary record to new testimonial or documentary evidence; a party seeking to re‑open must demonstrate why the evidence already before the Board is inadequate and show good cause why additional evidence is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel will consider whether parties had an adequate opportunity to address issues with the evidence already of record, whether additional briefing suffices, and how much additional time would be necessary to develop a new evidentiary record. The Board’s discovery rules govern testimonial evidence and cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional oral argument on remand
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, an additional oral hearing will not be authorized; normally the existing record and previous oral argument are sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The panel may authorize additional oral argument where new evidence is permitted or where necessary to afford due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default trial procedures for common remand scenarios (chart guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The SOP supplies default likelihoods (Additional Briefing / Additional Evidence / Oral Argument) for common remand scenarios: Erroneous Claim Interpretation; Failure to Consider the Evidence; Inadequate Explanation by the Board; Erroneous Application of Law; Lack of Due Process/Denial of APA rights; Improper Consideration of Arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Examples from the chart (interpretive, non-exhaustive):
- Erroneous Claim Interpretation: Additional briefing — 'Yes, unless the claim interpretation to be applied on remand was proposed by one of the parties and the effect thereof has been fully briefed'; Additional evidence — 'Yes, unless the evidence was fully briefed on the record'; Oral argument — 'No'.
- Failure to Consider the Evidence: Additional briefing — 'Yes, unless the evidence was fully briefed on the record'; Additional evidence — 'No, unless evidence of record is insufficient to afford due process'; Oral argument — 'No'.
- Inadequate Explanation by the Board: Additional briefing — 'No, unless the briefing on the issues is inadequate for the Board to have made a decision in the first instance'; Additional evidence — 'No'; Oral argument — 'No'.
- Erroneous Application of Law: Additional briefing — 'Yes, unless the law was fully briefed on the record but not reflected in Board decision'; Additional evidence — 'Yes'; Oral argument — 'No'.
- Lack of Due Process/Denial of APA rights: Additional briefing — 'Yes'; Additional evidence — 'Yes'; Oral argument — 'Yes, for parties whose rights have been violated, unless additional briefing on evidence of record is sufficient to afford due process.'
These particular remand scenarios are exemplary and do not reflect all possible outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel consideration of time/expense when reopening the record
rubrics_metrics.description: The panel will consider the time and expense involved that permitting additional briefing and new evidence will add to the proceeding and that reopening the record after remand may be inconsistent with the six‑month goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether additional briefing (without new evidence) may suffice to avoid reopening the record; consider downstream scheduling and discovery burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte and reexamination remand considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In ex parte appeals and reexamination appeals, reversals at the Federal Circuit are remanded to the PTO for further action; whether the Board or the examiner will take up remanded cases depends on (1) whether the Federal Circuit directed a particular part of the Office to act on remand, (2) whether outstanding rejections can be further addressed by the Board on the current record, and/or (3) whether a reversal requires further prior art searching by the examiner and/or issuance of a patent or reexamination certificate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although rare, the Board may ask the appellant or parties to provide further briefing; additional evidence is only permitted upon reopening of prosecution before the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default appeals procedures for ex parte/reexamination remand scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: The SOP provides default outcomes for common ex parte/reexamination remand scenarios (non‑exhaustive): e.g., for Erroneous Claim Interpretation — 'No, unless alternative claim interpretation renders the present rejection(s) moot'; Failure to Consider the Evidence — 'No, unless the evidence of record is deemed entirely insufficient to support the present rejection(s)'; Inadequate Explanation — 'No — the Board provides additional explanation or reverses on the present record'; Erroneous Application of Law — 'No, unless correct application of law renders rejections moot'; Lack of Due Process — 'Yes – typically in the form of a new ground of rejection'; Improper Consideration — 'No – arguments not sufficiently briefed before the Board are deemed waived.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedures are default and circumstances not contemplated may necessitate a different procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative examples to guide discretionary remand decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: SOP provides numerous case examples illustrating how panels have handled remands for erroneous claim interpretation, failure to consider evidence, inadequate explanation, erroneous application of law, lack of due process, and failure to consider arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels should use these examples to inform discretionary choices but treat examples as non‑binding illustrations of possible outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel expansion recommendation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels should consider recommending that the Chief Judge expand the panel, taking into account the factors expressed in SOP 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chief Judge may expand the panel for specific reasons (e.g., to address an issue of importance), but expansion is expected to be rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of precedential designation
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels should contemplate whether a decision on remand that involves novel, evolving, or contentious issues of law or policy might be considered for precedential designation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy considerations include whether the Federal Circuit’s decision highlights issues not limited to the particular case or of particular importance to the Office or patent community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling requests to stay remand proceedings pending certiorari
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent good cause, proceedings on remand generally will not be stayed once the Federal Circuit has issued its mandate, even when a party has petitioned the Supreme Court for certiorari. Parties may contact the Board to request authorization to file a motion to stay the remand proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will consider such requests on a case‑by‑case basis, may require briefing or decide by conference call, and the primary consideration is whether the Supreme Court’s judgment would impact the Board’s decision on remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing guidance regarding issuance of mandate and scheduling expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels and parties should be aware of the timing rules: under Fed. R. App. P. 41(b) a mandate 'must issue 7 days after the time to file a petition for rehearing expires,' and Fed. Cir. R. 40(e) allows 30 days for rehearing petitions; mandate typically issues about 37 days after judgment (longer in certain circumstances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This timing informs expectations for when the Board’s six‑month clock begins and when remand-related meetings and contacts should occur.
